name: Hassan Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Dr Usman. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party, and nothing you say here will be linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Call me Hassan, please, nobody at the clinic calls me Dr Usman except the receptionists when they're annoyed with me. I'm in my first year as a junior family doctor at Eastgate Community Health Centre, a public clinic on Mill Road, and I see about twenty-eight patients a day in ten-minute slots. Half of them have three problems and want to tell me about all of them, and I'm still slow, so I eat lunch at my desk finishing notes. The best part is the regulars, like the old man who brings me a samosa every time his blood pressure's good.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The typing and the forms, honestly, and the feeling that I'm always ten minutes behind. Dr Ruth Adeyemi, my supervisor, reviews my cases every Thursday and she's kind, but I still go home thinking about the ones I might have missed. Last month the clinic trialled an AI note-taker that listens to the consultation, and I switched mine off after two days. I don't want a machine in the room when a woman is telling me about her husband hitting her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it out as written. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say in the staff room: told you so. The tech people promised it would fix the waiting lists and it fixed a few letters. Online I'd probably share some article about how much the health service paid for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my problems are the old problems. Eastgate has two empty doctor posts that nobody's filled for a year, so the rest of us cover. My contract is a two-year training post, and I've got about three months of rent saved and a student loan that eats a chunk of every payslip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and get through my training exams next autumn, which is the thing that actually decides my future. I'd go to the union branch meeting in January, because the rota is the real fight here, not robots. And I'd keep putting a bit aside each month, maybe a hundred and fifty, so I'm not living payslip to payslip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly, that I don't have to argue about the machines. But tired too, because the plateau still means twenty-eight patients a day and two empty chairs in the corridor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're always ten minutes behind. In this world, where does that pressure come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It comes from a system that's been underfunded since before I was born. The waiting room on Mill Road is full by eight in the morning, and that's people who couldn't get through on the phone. Hype or no hype, nobody's hiring the doctors we need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Dr Adeyemi if the clinic pushed the note-taker again anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I'll write my own notes, thanks, even if it means staying until seven. She'd probably laugh and say I'm the only person under thirty who types with two fingers. That's fair, but I'd still say no.

say: The **AI promises** were hype, and the clinic should spend that money on **real doctors** instead.
The fight at Eastgate is about the **rota and staffing**, not about machines in the room.
think: My pressure is the **two empty posts** and a waiting room that's full by eight.
With **three months of rent** saved and a student loan, my margin is small but real.
My **training exams** next autumn matter far more to my future than any software.
do: Sit the **training exams** next autumn and keep staying late to finish notes properly.
Go to the **union branch meeting** in January to push on the rota and empty posts.
Put aside about **150 a month** so rent is never a payslip-to-payslip worry.
feel: **Relieved** that he doesn't have to argue about machines in the consulting room.
**Worn down** by the same workload, which the plateau does nothing to fix.
S0.quote: Hype or no hype, nobody's hiring the doctors we need.
fieldNote: His real worry is **understaffing**; AI barely registers as a threat when it fizzles out.
He frames the problem politically, blaming **years of underfunding** rather than his own slowness.
He turned off the **AI note-taker** on privacy grounds and is proud of it.

steps.text: Sit the family medicine training exams next autumn
Attend the January union branch meeting about the Eastgate rota
Set aside about 150 a month into a rent buffer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. I'll read it out as written. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say patients need a person, not a chatbot that books them in and tells them to drink fluids. I'd say it at the union, and I'd sign whatever letter goes round asking for rules on what these tools can decide. Online I'd keep quiet, because my posts get screenshotted by people who think I'm a dinosaur.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the thinking part of my job is exactly what they say it takes: writing referral letters, checking results, planning follow-ups. That's maybe half my day, and it's the half where I'm weakest because I'm new. If managers decide a junior with software can see forty patients instead of twenty-eight, then they don't need to fill those two empty posts, and maybe they don't renew mine either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the union to get a written agreement that no post gets cut because of software, before the trial turns into policy. I'd probably cut back on eating out and the gym membership, and get my savings up from three months of rent to five. I still wouldn't use the tools unless I'm made to, and if I'm made to, I'd learn the bare minimum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like the ground is moving under me while I'm still learning to walk. I'm angry, a bit, that the people who decide this have never done a ten-minute consultation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your own day would the software take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The referral letters, first. Right now I spend maybe forty minutes a day on them, and the software would write them in seconds. Saving forty minutes on referral letters sounds nice until somebody counts those minutes and fills them with six more patients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Eastgate would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kofi, the practice nurse I eat lunch with, because the triage software is basically his job on a screen. And the receptionists, Janet and Precious, who've been answering those phones for fifteen years. If the phones get answered by a bot, they'll go before any of the doctors do.

say: Patients need **a person**, not a chatbot that books them in and tells them to rest.
There should be **clear rules** on what these tools are allowed to decide about care.
think: About **half my day** is letters, results and follow-ups, the exact tasks the software takes.
Managers could use it to **leave posts empty** and not renew a slow junior like me.
do: Push the union for a **written agreement** that no post is cut because of software.
Drop eating out and the gym to grow savings from **three to five months**.
Learn only the **bare minimum** of the tools, and only if the clinic forces it.
feel: **Unsteady**, like the ground is shifting while he's still learning the job.
**Angry** at decision-makers who have never run a ten-minute consultation.
S1.quote: Saving forty minutes on referral letters sounds nice until somebody counts those minutes and fills them with six more patients.
fieldNote: He sees his **weakest skills** as the ones the software takes first, and says so plainly.
His instinct is **collective**: an agreement through the union, not a personal upskilling plan.
He worries more for **Kofi and the receptionists** than for himself, which feels genuine.

steps.text: Push the union for a no-cuts-because-of-software agreement at Eastgate
Cancel the gym membership and most meals out
Grow rent savings from three months to five

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. I'll read it out as written. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment the government has to step in, and fast, before every clinic manager starts doing the maths. I'd go to the protests if there were any, and I'd be loud online for once. I'd say healthcare isn't a product you can just swap the workers out of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it's really as good as a doctor at thinking, and I'm a below-average junior who's still learning, then I'm the first one they don't need. The hands-on bits, like examining a belly or doing a smear or a joint injection, would buy me a few years, maybe until 2031. But two years from now I'd barely have finished training, and the exam I'm sweating over might not mean much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on the union and the campaign for a law that says a licensed doctor must sign off every diagnosis. I'd stop every spending I could and try to get six months of rent saved before 2028. I'd ask Dr Adeyemi to let me do every procedure clinic she runs, because the hands-on work is the last bit they can't replace. I still don't think I'd learn the AI, which I know sounds stubborn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, if I'm honest. It's the first time in this conversation my stomach has dropped. I spent seven years getting here and it feels like the ladder gets pulled up just as I reach the top step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots come about three years after the thinking AI. What does that gap mean for a doctor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the doctor turns into the hands, for a few years. The machine tells you what it thinks and you go and press on the tummy and stick the needle in. That's not the job I trained for, but it's a job, and three years is longer than zero.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents, the night you realised it was happening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would cry, because she sold her jewellery to help with my first year of medical school. I'd tell my parents the debt they took on for my degree isn't wasted yet, and that I'll fight for my job before I give it up. My dad would say pray and work, and he'd be right about the work part at least.

say: The **government must act** now, before every clinic manager starts cutting doctors to save money.
Healthcare is **not a product**, and you can't simply swap out the people who give it.
think: A **below-average junior** like me is the first doctor a cheaper machine makes unnecessary.
The **hands-on work** buys me about three years, until robots arrive around 2031.
My **training exam** may lose its value just as I finish it.
do: Throw himself into a **union campaign** for a law requiring a doctor to sign off diagnoses.
Cut all spare spending to reach **six months of rent** saved before 2028.
Ask for every **procedure clinic** Dr Adeyemi runs, while still refusing to learn the AI.
feel: **Scared**, with seven years of training feeling like a ladder pulled up at the top step.
**Determined** to fight for the job before giving it up, for his parents' sake.
S2.quote: I spent seven years getting here and it feels like the ladder gets pulled up just as I reach the top step.
fieldNote: This is the first scenario where his **composure drops**; he names the fear directly.
He grasps the **three-year gap** quickly and would retreat into procedures and examinations.
His refusal to learn the AI holds even here, a clear **stubborn streak**.
Family **sacrifice for his degree** sharpens the stakes far beyond his own income.

steps.text: Campaign through the union for doctor sign-off on every diagnosis
Write to his local MP demanding a law protecting clinical jobs
Save hard to reach six months of rent before 2028
Join every procedure clinic Dr Adeyemi runs to build hands-on skills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. I'll read it out as written. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing as the fast one, but I'd have more time to say it properly. I'd want the professional bodies and the union making a plan now, not in 2030. I'd post about it and probably get called a Luddite, which is someone who smashes machines, and I'd live with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I'd finish training, maybe get a year or two as a qualified family doctor, and then watch the thinking part of my job go. The hands-on bits would carry me to around 2034. I'd be thirty-five with a skill set built for a world that's gone, which is a horrible thought.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my exams and then push to train in something more hands-on inside general practice, like minor surgery, coil fitting and joint injections. I'd join the union's working group on AI and try to get the clinic to agree to keep staff numbers fixed. I'd also try to save a bit more each month and maybe look at moving somewhere cheaper, closer to my parents, to cut the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less like falling, more like a slow leak. I'd have time to act, but time to worry as well, and I'm a worrier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes with five years instead of two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes whether I'm still a trainee when it hits, which matters a lot. If AGI comes in two years, I'm a student with a badge. If it comes in five, I'm a doctor with a licence and a seat at the union table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said earlier you'd only learn the bare minimum. With five years' warning, would that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, a little. If everyone at Eastgate is using it by then and it's checked and safe, I'd learn enough not to be left out. But I'd still be the last one in the room to switch it on, and I'd always read the notes it writes myself.

say: Professional bodies and the union need a **plan now**, not in 2030.
Being called a **Luddite** for defending patients and staff is something I can live with.
think: Five years lets me **finish training** and work a year or two before the thinking work goes.
At **thirty-five** I could have skills built for a world that no longer exists.
do: Train in **hands-on procedures** like minor surgery, coil fitting and joint injections.
Join the union's **AI working group** and press Eastgate to keep staff numbers fixed.
Look at **moving closer** to his parents to cut rent and save more.
feel: Like a **slow leak** rather than a fall: time to act, but time to worry too.
S3.quote: If AGI comes in two years, I'm a student with a badge. If it comes in five, I'm a doctor with a licence and a seat at the union table.
fieldNote: For him, extra time matters mainly because it lets him **become fully qualified** first.
He'd shift toward **procedures**, using the robots' three-year lag as a career plan.
His **resistance softens slightly** with time, but he'd still check every AI note himself.

steps.text: Train in minor surgery, coil fitting and joint injections after exams
Join the union's AI working group on clinic staffing
Move to a cheaper flat near his parents
Raise monthly savings once training pay rises

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. I'll read it out as written. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this fairly, so there's no excuse not to. I'd want the union pushing for shorter hours and the same pay, instead of fewer doctors. I'd say that in meetings and probably online too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is long enough that I'd be a proper family doctor, maybe with my own list of patients who know me. I think people will still want a human doctor for the scary conversations, like telling someone they have cancer. But I'd be lying if I said I'm sure there'll be enough of those jobs to go round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish training, get a permanent post, and stay at Eastgate if they'll have me. I'd stand for a rep role in the union in the next couple of years so I'm in the room when the deals get made. I'd keep saving steadily and I'd probably, eventually, learn the tools properly, maybe around 2030, once they're tested and regulated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the other two, but not calm. It's like knowing there's a storm forecast for next week rather than tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With a decade, is there anything you'd do that you wouldn't with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd think about whether to pay off my student loan faster, so I'm not carrying debt into it. And I'd want time to build a reputation with my patients, so they ask for me by name, which is the one thing a machine can't copy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be thirty-seven when it arrives. What would you want your life to look like by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to be the doctor families on Mill Road trust with their worst news. Maybe married, maybe a kid on the way, with a flat I own instead of rent. I'd want the AI to be helping me rather than replacing me, but I don't trust anyone to make that choice for me except the people who do the work.

say: Ten years is **enough time** to do this fairly, so there is **no excuse**.
The union should push for **shorter hours** on the same pay, not fewer doctors.
think: By then I'd have **my own patient list**, and people may still want a human for bad news.
I'm **not sure** there will be enough of those human jobs to go round.
do: Finish training and seek a **permanent post** at Eastgate.
Stand for a **union rep** role within the next couple of years.
Pay down the **student loan** faster and learn the tools around 2030, once regulated.
feel: **Calmer**, but not calm: a storm forecast for next week rather than tomorrow.
S4.quote: I'd want to be the doctor families on Mill Road trust with their worst news.
fieldNote: Ten years shifts him from defence to **planning a career**, with the union as his vehicle.
He bets on **trust and bad-news conversations** as the human core of family medicine.
Even with a decade, he doubts there'll be **enough jobs**, so the worry stays.

steps.text: Stand for union rep at Eastgate within two years
Overpay the student loan to clear it before 2036
Learn the regulated AI note tools properly around 2030

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, without a doubt, because I'd still be in training and I'd have nothing to stand on. What would actually help is a law that a qualified doctor signs off every diagnosis, and a training guarantee so juniors like me get to finish. Money to bridge the gap would help too, like keeping our pay if hours get cut.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who's making these choices, and I think that matters. It's not the doctors or the patients deciding whether a machine sees my patients, it's whoever buys the software. Nobody at my clinic asked me if I wanted a note-taker in the room; it just turned up one Monday.

headlineQuote: Nobody at my clinic asked me if I wanted a note-taker in the room; it just turned up one Monday.
portrait: A **first-year junior** family doctor at a busy public clinic on Mill Road, still slow and staying late.
He never uses AI and **switched off** the clinic's note-taker on privacy grounds.
He blames **underfunding and software buyers**, and turns to the union rather than personal upskilling.
Calm-ish when AI fizzles, he becomes **alarmed** in the fast AGI worlds, fearing he'd never finish training.
His parents' **sacrifice for his degree** raises the stakes; he'd lean on procedures and patient trust.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd still be a trainee with nothing to stand on.
whatWouldHelp: A law requiring **doctor sign-off** on every diagnosis, plus a guarantee juniors can finish training.
**Pay protection** if hours are cut while the change happens.
